core: Working definition: a dietary supplement is a product taken by mouth that contains a dietary ingredient intended to supplement the diet (FDA working definition, rooted in DSHEA 1994)
Dietary ingredients include vitamins, minerals, herbs and other botanicals, amino acids, and dietary substances such as enzymes and probiotics
Common forms: pills (tablets), capsules, powders, liquids, and gummies, each with an original one-line example (also softgels, bars, drinks per FDA)

U.S. regulation: the FDA regulates dietary supplements as foods, not drugs, under DSHEA (1994); no premarket approval for safety or effectiveness; manufacturers responsible for safety and truthful labels
FDA post-market authority: FDA can take action against adulterated or misbranded supplements after they reach the market
Supplement Facts panel: required label listing serving size, dietary ingredients, amount per serving, and percent Daily Value where established
Honest note: supplements cannot replace a varied diet (FDA: supplements should not take the place of the variety of foods important for a healthy diet)
Claims problem: products can make claims; claims are not proof; only drugs may claim to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease; structure/function claims carry an FDA disclaimer
Honest framing: supplements are bridges, not foundations; the varied diet is the foundation
supporting: Medicines must be FDA-approved for safety and effectiveness before sale; supplements do not require this
Structure/function claims must carry the disclaimer that the statement has not been evaluated by the FDA
Products intended to treat, diagnose, cure, or prevent disease are drugs even if labeled as supplements
Original worked example comparing a gummy multivitamin (Supplement Facts panel) with a structure/function claim label
Many U.S. adults and children take one or more vitamins or other dietary supplements

claims.claim: The working definition of a dietary supplement (per DSHEA 1994, stated by the FDA): a product intended for ingestion that contains a dietary ingredient intended to supplement the diet; dietary ingredients include vitamins, minerals, herbs and other botanicals, amino acids, and other dietary substances such as enzymes and live microbials (probiotics).

Dietary supplements are taken by mouth and come in many forms, including pills/tablets, capsules, powders, liquids, and gummies (FDA also lists softgels, gel caps, bars, and drinks; MedlinePlus lists pills, capsules, powders, drinks, and energy bars).

In the United States, the FDA regulates dietary supplements as foods, not as drugs, under the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 (DSHEA), under a different set of regulations than those covering conventional foods and drug products.

Unlike drugs, dietary supplements do not receive premarket FDA approval for safety or effectiveness; manufacturers and distributors are responsible for evaluating the safety and labeling of their products before marketing, and the FDA has authority to take action against adulterated or misbranded supplements after they reach the market.

Products sold as dietary supplements carry a Supplement Facts label/panel that lists the serving size, the dietary ingredients in the product, the amount per serving, and the percent Daily Value where established, plus other ingredients such as fillers, binders, and flavorings.

The FDA advises that supplements should not take the place of the variety of foods that are important for a healthy diet; a varied diet remains the foundation that supplements are meant to add to, not replace.

Supplement labels may carry health claims, nutrient content claims, or structure/function claims; only drugs may legally claim to diagnose, cure, mitigate, treat, or prevent a disease, and structure/function claims must carry the disclaimer that the statement has not been evaluated by the FDA and the product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease. A claim on a label is a statement, not proof of effect.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether supplements can substitute for food
positions: Supplement marketing often frames products as a convenient way to get nutrients, implying a pill can stand in for food
Authoritative sources (FDA) state that supplements should not take the place of the variety of foods important for a healthy diet
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Sources agree supplements can help meet specific nutrient needs but do not replace a varied diet. The lesson teaches the honest note (bridges, not foundations) and offers no purchase or dosing advice.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether supplements are approved by the FDA like drugs
positions: Consumers often assume a product on the shelf has been checked and approved by a federal agency before sale
Under DSHEA, supplements are regulated as foods with no premarket approval for safety or effectiveness; FDA acts after marketing against adulterated or misbranded products
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Sources agree on the DSHEA facts. The lesson states the approval gap plainly and factually, without scare content.

sourceRecords.title: Questions and Answers on Dietary Supplements
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Confirms Congress defined 'dietary supplement' in DSHEA (1994); the definition (product intended for ingestion that contains a dietary ingredient intended to supplement the diet); the dietary ingredient list (vitamins, minerals, herbs/botanicals, amino acids, dietary substances such as enzymes and probiotics); forms (pills, tablets, capsules, gummies, softgels, liquids, powders; bars/teas only if labeled as supplements); and the requirement that structure/function claims carry the disclaimer 'This statement has not been evaluated by the FDA. This product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.'

sourceRecords.title: FDA 101: Dietary Supplements
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Consumer update confirming supplements are intended to add to or supplement the diet; forms include tablets, capsules, soft gels, gel caps, powders, bars, gummies, and liquids; Supplement Facts label with serving size, servings per container, dietary ingredients and amounts; 'supplements should not take the place of the variety of foods that are important for a healthy diet'; and the rule that a product intended to treat, diagnose, cure, or prevent disease is a drug even if labeled as a supplement.

sourceRecords.title: Dietary Supplements (FDA topic page)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. FDA topic page: FDA regulates both finished dietary supplement products and dietary ingredients under a different set of regulations than those covering 'conventional' foods and drug products; under DSHEA, manufacturers and distributors are prohibited from marketing adulterated or misbranded products and are responsible for evaluating safety and labeling before marketing; FDA has authority to take action against any adulterated or misbranded supplement product after it reaches the market.

sourceRecords.title: Dietary Supplements: Background Information (Fact Sheet for Consumers)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. ODS background factsheet: DSHEA definition of a dietary supplement (intended to supplement the diet; contains one or more dietary ingredients; taken by mouth as a pill, capsule, tablet, or liquid; labeled on the front panel as a dietary supplement); 'Although dietary supplements are regulated by the FDA as foods, they are regulated differently from other foods and from drugs'; no provisions for FDA to approve supplements for safety or effectiveness before they reach the consumer; FDA must prove a marketed product unsafe to restrict or remove it; three claim types (health claim, nutrient content claim, structure/function claim); structure/function claims cannot mention a specific disease and must carry the FDA disclaimer.

sourceRecords.title: Dietary Supplements: What You Need to Know (Fact Sheet for Consumers)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. ODS consumer factsheet: many adults and children in the U.S. take one or more vitamins or other dietary supplements; supplements can contain vitamins, minerals, herbs or other botanicals, amino acids, enzymes, and many other ingredients; forms include tablets, capsules, gummies, powders, drinks, and energy bars; the Supplement Facts label lists active ingredients, amount per serving (dose), and other ingredients such as fillers, binders, and flavorings; medicines must be FDA-approved before sale but supplements do not require this approval; supplement companies are responsible for evidence that products are safe and that label claims are truthful and not misleading.

sourceRecords.title: Dietary Supplements (Health Topics)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. MedlinePlus health topic: dietary supplements are vitamins, minerals, herbs, and many other products; they can come as pills, capsules, powders, drinks, and energy bars; supplements do not have to go through the testing that drugs do; some supplements can play an important role in health (e.g., calcium and vitamin D for strong bones).
